every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited

claims.claim: Acamprosate, a small fully ionized polar acid, has absolute oral bioavailability of approximately 11% in humans, providing a transferable direct low-F outcome for highly polar ionized acids.
Ferulic acid, a low-lipophilicity carboxylic acid, shows 3-10% oral bioavailability in humans, supporting low F for polar carboxylic acid-containing molecules.
The query is a fully ionized dicarboxylic acid diketopiperazine (logD -5.3, TPSA 191, 6 HBD/6 HBA), consistent with the low-permeability absorption liabilities of these low-F analogs.
High-F oseltamivir records (79-94%) are not transferable because oseltamivir is an ester prodrug that masks a carboxylate; the query has free carboxylic acids and no prodrug masking.
A conflicting acamprosate report of 42% is outweighed by the absolute bioavailability estimates of approximately 11% and does not undermine the low-F transfer.

evidence_gaps: No direct oral bioavailability or matched oral-versus-IV exposure data exist for the query molecule.
No direct ChEMBL evidence for the query; assessment relies on physicochemical priors and analog transfer.
Transfer from acamprosate and ferulic acid is analog-based; differences in molecular weight, DKP scaffold, and possible active transport or prodrug behavior are unquantified.
No formulation, solubility/dissolution, permeability, or first-pass data are available for the query.
Conflicting acamprosate bioavailability reports (e.g., 42%) and variable indoramin data limit quantitative extrapolation.
content.decision_summary: Predicted low because the query is a fully ionized, extremely polar dicarboxylic acid DKP (logD -5.3, TPSA 191) and the most transferable direct human low-F contexts—acamprosate (~11%) and ferulic acid (3-10%)—support F<20%; high-F oseltamivir evidence is not transferable due to prodrug masking.
